findings.summary: The base arm's value labels use a (10, 24) point offset, which puts '18.96' directly above-right of the one-lane marker and into the rising grey line: on the rendered PNG the label box (x 216-275, y 538-554) contains 11 pixels of the #929292 line and the nearest text pixel is 2.2 px from it, so a dash grazes the top-right of the text. The digits remain readable and nothing is obscured, so this does not stop a reader, but the label is the only one on the canvas that the data run into; moving it below-left of the marker, or lifting the offset above the line's local slope, would clear it.

The 'batched' arm's labels use a (52, 12) point offset against the base arm's (10, 24), so '31.80' is drawn about 72 px - roughly 1.2 lanes - to the right of its marker, at about x = 17.2 in data units while the marker sits at lane 16. A reader has to infer which marker it belongs to from colour alone, and its position falls in the empty stretch of axis beyond the last measurement, where a value could be read as belonging to a lane that was never run. The label also sits above the line's y at that x, so it does not obviously annotate the endpoint. A consistent small offset for both arms would remove the ambiguity.

The x axis is ticked at 1, 4, 8, 12 and 16 but only lanes 1 and 16 were measured, and each arm is drawn as one straight segment between those two points. The ticks at 4, 8 and 12 therefore mark lane counts with no data under them, so the panel reads as a measured scaling curve sampled at five lane counts rather than as two endpoints joined by a straight line. The page's alt text and caption do say one and sixteen lanes, and the numeric table beside it carries only those two rows, so the reader who consults the page is corrected; the picture alone is not. Ticking only the measured lanes, or marking the segment as an interpolation, would make the figure honest on its own.
